newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel releases ethics recommendations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel releases ethics recommendations.

text.p: A U.S. House task force released recommendations Thursday for improving the ethics review process.

The 12-member task force, co-chaired by Representative Bob Livingston, a Republican from Louisiana, and Representative Benjamin Cardin, a Maryland Democrat, was set up after the House's difficult experience in resolving the ethics case involving House Speaker Newt Gingrich.
In Gingrich's ethics case, he said he had not done anything intentionally wrong but said in December he brought discredit to the House. He was fined $300,000.
"I believe this is a good product. I believe it is about as good a bipartisan product that we can arrive at," Livingston said.
A hearing on the new recommendations is scheduled for Friday. No floor action is likely until at least next month.

The task force proposals would expand the number of House members involved in ethics investigations, set time limits for action on the complaints, give the senior minority party member of the panel the right to place an item on the agenda, and establish that the staff is nonpartisan.

It provides for more secrecy for the investigative aspects of the panel's work, although the actual adjudication sessions would be public. And it allows people outside Congress to file complaints if they have direct knowledge of wrongdoing.
They could not make such a complaint based on a news report but could base their allegations on information received by someone else.
The recommendations were originally set to have been made public Wednesday, when Livingston cancelled a scheduled bipartisan news conference but signalled that Cardin should feel free to proceed.
Gingrich's office said the delay had been at the request of some House members who wanted to slow down the process.

Representative Bill Thomas, a California Republican who voted against the report, said it would allow complaints to be made on the basis of hearsay. He said subjects of complaints could be left in limbo indefinitely, with their political careers in jeopardy.
Cardin said Wednesday that 11 of the 12 task force members had backed the plan.
In fact, eight voted for it; Thomas voted against it, and three other Republicans who were not present for the vote but were consulted later "will have to speak for themselves," Livingston said.
While the task force worked, there was a moratorium on new ethics complaints. That expires next Tuesday.
